circ.title: Natural circulation in a drum boiler
caption: Natural circulation. Water falls down the unheated downcomer, is heated in the evaporator tubes in the gas path, partly boils, and the lighter steam-water mixture rises back to the drum. No pump drives it. Switch on the load step to see swell: pressure dips, more water flashes to steam, and the bubbles push the drum level up even though water is being used faster.
circ.alt: A drum boiler: water falls down an unheated downcomer and rises, partly boiling, through heated evaporator tubes back to the drum.

Pressure recovers; bubbles shrink; level settles back
Steady circulation: down the downcomer, up the heated tubes

expand.title: Pipe thermal expansion
caption: A 30 m steam pipe held by a fixed point (anchor) at the left and sliding supports elsewhere. As it heats, it grows away from the anchor; each support slides by an amount proportional to its distance from the anchor. The expansion indicator at the free end shows the total growth. Movement is drawn about 45 times larger than life.
expand.alt: A steam pipe anchored at the left end on sliding supports, growing to the right as it heats, with an expansion indicator at the free end.
expand.status: {temp} °C: the pipe is {dmm} mm longer than cold (30 m × 1.2×10⁻⁵ /K × {dk} K)

wall.title: Heating a thick drum wall
caption: Simplified one-dimensional estimate for a 125 mm steel wall heated from the inside and insulated outside (thermal diffusivity about 1.1×10⁻⁵ m²/s). The faster the inside heats, the bigger the temperature difference across the wall, and thermal stress grows with that difference. Real drums add nozzles and top-to-bottom differences.
wall.alt: A section through a 125 mm drum wall, coloured by temperature, beside a chart of temperature across the wall while the inside heats.

gate.title: Gate valve cutaway
caption: Rising-stem gate valve. Drag the slider or press play. The gate slides straight across the flow and wedges between two seats; most of the flow returns in the first part of the stroke, which is why gate valves are for isolation, not throttling.
gate.alt: Cutaway of a rising-stem gate valve in a pipe: handwheel, stem, packing, bonnet, a gate that slides down between two seats, and water flowing through.

safety.title: Spring-loaded safety valve
caption: Spring-loaded safety valve. Pressure under the disc rises until it overcomes the spring at the set pressure; the valve pops fully open, blows, and reseats only when pressure has fallen a few percent below set (the blowdown). The adjusting screw sets the spring force and so the set pressure.
safety.alt: Spring-loaded safety valve beside a chart of the pressure under its disc: the disc lifts at the set pressure and reseats a few percent below it.

status.text: Pressure {p:1}% of set · OPEN, blowing to outlet
Pressure {p:1}% of set · reseated below set (blowdown)
Pressure {p:1}% of set · closed, spring holds the disc

pump.title: Centrifugal pump
caption: Centrifugal pump seen along the shaft. Water enters at the eye in the centre, the spinning vanes throw it outwards, and the volute (the widening spiral casing) turns that speed into pressure at the discharge. Switch on cavitation to see vapour bubbles form where pressure is lowest, near the eye, and collapse against the vanes further out.
pump.alt: Centrifugal pump seen along its shaft: water enters at the eye, the impeller vanes throw it outwards and the volute leads it to the discharge.

status.text: Cavitation: pressure at the eye falls below vapour pressure; bubbles form, then implode (red) as pressure rises, pitting the vanes
Normal: water speeds up through the vanes; the volute turns speed into pressure

orifice.title: Orifice flowmeter and Bernoulli
caption: Flow through an orifice plate. In the narrow jet just after the plate the water speeds up and its pressure drops (Bernoulli); the columns show pressure at three points. The drop measured between the tappings rises with the square of flow, so at 25% flow the DP is only about 6% of full scale. Some pressure is never recovered: that is the meter's permanent loss.
orifice.alt: Water flowing through an orifice plate, with three pressure columns: before the plate, just after it, and downstream.
orifice.status: Flow {v100}% → DP {dp}% of full scale (DP ∝ flow²)

gauge.title: Drum level gauge faults
caption: A local bi-colour gauge connected to the drum by a steam line and a water line. Pick a fault: a leak on the steam side makes the gauge read high, a leak on the water side makes it read low, and a blocked connection freezes it while the real level keeps moving.
gauge.alt: A drum and a local bi-colour level gauge joined by a steam line and a water line, with the real and the gauge level side by side.

status.text: Normal: gauge follows the drum level
Blocked: gauge FROZEN while the real level moves

title: Start here
goals: Know what this course is for, who should take it, and how to skip what you already know.

q: A guess before you start. The HRSG manual says LP steam pressure is "0.44 MPa (gauge indication)" in one place and "0.44 MPa.a" in another. Does it matter?

why: Gauge pressure is measured from the atmosphere, absolute from a perfect vacuum. They differ by about 0.1 MPa, which is almost 25% here. Module 2 covers this.

text: Yes, they differ by about 0.1 MPa, roughly a quarter of the value here.
why: Right. At high pressure the difference hardly matters; at LP it matters a lot. The design data table is explicit (absolute), so these courses use 0.44 MPa absolute. Module 2 covers this.
It matters for every reading, including the boiling temperature you expect.

p: Start with
(course 1), which covers the whole plant. This course is course 2; its placement test will let you skip what course 1 already taught you.
The

and the manual it is built on assume you already know how a combined-cycle plant works, what the equipment is called, how instruments measure, and how a shift is run. This course teaches exactly those assumptions and nothing else. It was built by going through the HRSG course line by line and listing every term and idea it uses without explaining. That list is on the
page.
By the end you should be able to open the HRSG course and follow every sentence. More concretely, you should be able to:

ul: Sketch the combined cycle and say where the HRSG, the three-way damper, the condenser and the feed pumps sit.
Convert between gauge and absolute pressure, t/h and kg/s, and read a drum level in millimetres from a datum.
Explain boiling, saturation, superheat, flashing, swell and shrink, and natural circulation.
Explain why thick metal must be heated slowly and why pipes need room to grow.
Name each HRSG component and valve type and say what it does.
Explain how level, flow, pressure and temperature are measured, and how a DCS, an interlock and a trip differ.
Say what each water chemistry parameter protects against.
Follow a work permit, take and repeat back an order, and read a P&ID, a KKS code and this manual's translated English.

p: The
tests this with questions written in the HRSG course's own language.
Take the

first. It has two questions per module. Where you get both right, you can skip that module. Mechanical and chemical engineers often skip Modules 3 and 4; electrical and control engineers often skip Module 7; everyone should do Module 10, because the manual's English is unusual.

cards: Each module opens with a question before any teaching. Answer it anyway.
Worked examples reveal one step at a time. Predict each step first.
Each module ends with questions phrased like the HRSG course, so you know you're ready for it.
Short daily drill on the equipment and terms. Five minutes a day.

small: Plant: Al-Rumailah Combined Cycle 730 MW. The HRSG course covers the Dongfang Lingri MHDB-SGT5-4000F-Q1 HRSG behind a Siemens SGT5-4000F gas turbine.

title: The combined cycle in one picture
goals: Sketch the flow from air to electricity through GT, HRSG and steam turbine.
Explain why exhaust heat is worth recovering and why there are three pressure levels and a reheat.
Say what "2×1", the bypass stack, turbine bypass and condenser vacuum mean.

q: Guess: why doesn't the plant simply use one very high-pressure boiler section in the HRSG?

why: The HP section already runs at about 12.4 MPa safely.

text: Once the gas cools below HP boiling temperature, HP water can't take any more heat, so lower-pressure sections recover what's left.
why: Right. That is why there are HP, IP and LP sections, each boiling at a lower temperature.

text: The steam turbine needs three different steams for balance.
why: The turbine uses them, but the reason for three levels is heat recovery from the cooling gas.

p: The
(GT) compresses air, burns fuel gas in it, and expands the hot gas through a turbine that drives a generator. It still throws away gas at about
. The
(heat recovery steam generator) uses that hot exhaust to boil water into steam. The
(ST) expands the steam to drive a second generator. The
turns the used steam back into water, and pumps send that water back to the HRSG. That loop is the steam cycle.
The HRSG has no burner of its own on this plant ("no supplementary firing"). Every kilowatt it produces comes from GT exhaust, so HRSG output follows GT load.

h: Why three pressures and a reheat

p: Hot gas can boil high-pressure water, but high-pressure water boils at a high temperature (about
at the HP drum's pressure). Once the gas has cooled below that, it can no longer boil HP water. A second, lower-pressure section (IP, boils near
) takes the next slice of heat, and a third (LP, near
) the next. Three levels squeeze more heat out of the gas before it leaves the stack.
steam that has done work in the HP turbine comes back ("cold reheat"), goes through the HRSG's
to about
again ("hot reheat") and goes to the IP turbine. This raises output and keeps the steam dry for longer in the turbine.

ul: two or three gas turbines, each with its own HRSG, feeding one steam turbine through common steam headers. Joining a second HRSG to steam that is already on line is called "combining steam".
a large flap between GT and HRSG. It sends exhaust either into the HRSG or straight up a bypass stack, letting the GT run alone (simple cycle) with the HRSG isolated.

valves that send HRSG steam around the steam turbine straight to the condenser (after cooling it with spray water). Used at startup, shutdown and trips, so the HRSG can make steam when the turbine can't take it.

the condenser runs far below atmospheric pressure. "Vacuum 80 kPa" means 80 kPa below atmosphere, about 21 kPa absolute. Lower pressure means the steam turbine can extract more work, and it is needed before the bypasses can dump steam there.

case: Operators say "the HRSG follows the GT". What does that mean in practice when the GT load drops from 100% to 60%?
steps: No supplementary firing, so all HRSG heat is GT exhaust.
Less exhaust flow and usually lower exhaust temperature, so less heat reaches the HRSG.
Less steam is produced. Pressures fall (the plant runs "sliding pressure"), steam temperatures may shift, and the spray-water control has to respond.

Drum levels (a pressure change moves the level, Module 3), steam temperatures and the spray valves. This is why the HRSG course lists "GT load and exhaust temperature variation" as a cause of steam temperature change.

q: What is the three-way damper for?

why: It is fully open or fully closed and doesn't control temperature.

text: To send GT exhaust either into the HRSG or up the bypass stack.
why: Correct. With gas to the bypass stack, the GT runs in simple cycle and the HRSG is isolated.

text: To mix fresh air with the exhaust.

q: What does the turbine bypass do?

text: Sends HRSG steam around the steam turbine to the condenser.
why: Right. Used when the turbine can't take steam (startup, shutdown, trips).
That is the three-way damper and bypass stack.

text: Returns water from the condenser to the HRSG.

q: Where does reheated steam go?

why: The HP turbine gets HP main steam. Its exhaust is cold reheat.
Correct: cold reheat from the HP turbine is reheated in the HRSG and goes to the IP turbine.

q: "Condenser vacuum 85 kPa" means the absolute pressure in the condenser is about:

why: Vacuum is measured down from atmospheric (about 101 kPa).
Vacuum is below atmospheric, not above.

title: Bridge to the HRSG course
intro: These come straight from the HRSG course and manual. If you can answer them, you are ready for the parts of that course that rely on this module.

q: HRSG course: "The bypass line only can be used when the vacuum pump runs normally and condenser vacuum is more than 80 kPa." Why?

text: The turbine bypass dumps steam into the condenser, which must be under good vacuum to take it.
why: Right. Without vacuum the condenser can't condense the dumped steam.

text: The bypass stack needs vacuum to draw gas.
why: This is the steam turbine bypass, not the gas bypass stack.

text: Vacuum keeps the drum level stable.
why: Drum level is not the reason.

q: HRSG course: "Before the second main engine is combined with steam, the first is reduced to the minimum stable combustion load." What is being combined?

text: A second HRSG's steam into the header already feeding the steam turbine.
why: Correct. In a 2×1 or 3×1 plant, each HRSG joins the common steam headers.

text: The HP and IP steam in one HRSG.

title: Units and how to read a number
goals: Convert between gauge and absolute pressure, MPa, bar, kPa and mmH₂O.
Convert t/h to kg/s and use rates in °C/min and MPa/min.
Read a drum level in mm from a datum, and read ppm, ppb, µS/cm, MΩ and Nm³/min.

q: Guess: a local gauge reads 0.44 MPa. What is the absolute pressure?

why: Local gauges read gauge pressure, relative to the atmosphere.
Add about 0.1 MPa for the atmosphere.
You add the atmosphere to gauge pressure, not subtract.

p: pressure is measured from a perfect vacuum.
pressure is measured from the surrounding atmosphere, which is about
. So:
absolute ≈ gauge + 0.1 MPa
The manual writes "MPa.a" for absolute and "MPa(g)" or "gauge indication" for gauge. Often it writes plain "MPa" and you have to work out which. Local gauges read gauge pressure. At the HP drum (
) the 0.1 hardly matters; for LP steam (
, about 0.34 MPa on a gauge) it is almost a quarter of the value.

head: Unit
Equals

p: Steam and water flows are usually in
(tonnes per hour). Gas flow is in
. To convert:
. HP steam 279 t/h = 77.5 kg/s. Air flows use
: cubic metres per minute at "normal" conditions (0 °C, 1 atm), so different machines can be compared.
Startup limits are rates:
for heating,
for pressure. To check a rate, divide the change by the time. To plan, divide the total change by the rate: heating a drum from 100 °C to 327 °C at 5 °C/min takes at least
Drum level is in mm from a reference line (the
), often the drum centreline or a point below it. It is not the depth of water. "−50 mm" means 50 mm below the datum. "NWL+100" means 100 mm above the normal water level.

case: The HRSG course flags that the HP high-pressure alarm is 12.3 MPa while the drum working pressure is 12.44 MPa.a. Could both be right?
steps: 12.44 is marked absolute. 12.3 has no mark.
If 12.3 is gauge, then absolute is 12.3 + 0.1 = 12.4 MPa.a.
12.4 MPa.a is essentially the working pressure, so an alarm there would sound at normal operation.

Unit confusion explains part of the gap but not all of it. The alarm still looks too low, which is why the HRSG course says to get the real setpoint from the DCS. Always ask "gauge or absolute?" before comparing two pressures.

q: Convert 181.5 t/h (HP feed pump rated flow) to kg/s.
A drum heats from 150 °C to 250 °C in 25 minutes. The limit is 5 °C/min. Within limit?
Drum level reads "−450 mm". What does that mean?

text: There is 450 mm of water in the drum.
why: Level is measured from a datum, not from the bottom.

text: The water surface is 450 mm below the level datum.

why: It is below the datum, not empty.

q: Which unit tells you about dissolved salts in water?

why: Dissolved salts carry electric current, so conductivity rises with them.
pH is acidity, not total salts.

q: 3 bar gauge is how many MPa absolute?

why: That is gauge. Add the atmosphere.

title: Bridge to the HRSG course
intro: These come straight from the HRSG course and manual. If you can answer them, you are ready for the parts of that course that rely on this module.

q: HRSG course: "Raise pressure at 0.1–0.3 MPa/min." The test pressure is 4.0 MPa. What is the shortest time to reach it from zero?

why: 4.0 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 13.3 minutes at the fastest allowed rate (plus the hold at 10%).
That is at 0.1 MPa/min, the slowest end of the range.

q: HRSG course: HP steam flow 279 t/h, feedwater 305 t/h. How big is the mismatch in kg/s?

why: 26 t/h ÷ 3.6 ≈ 7.2 kg/s, a big mismatch that needs explaining.

title: Water and steam
goals: Use the saturation curve: boiling temperature depends on pressure.
Explain superheat, latent heat, flashing and condensation.
Explain swell and shrink, and how natural circulation works.

q: Guess: the HP drum pressure is 12.44 MPa absolute. What is the water temperature in it?

why: 100 °C is boiling at atmospheric pressure only.
At 12.44 MPa water boils at about 327 °C, and a drum is full of boiling water.
That is the superheated steam leaving the superheater, not drum water.

p: Water boils at 100 °C only at atmospheric pressure. Raise the pressure and it boils hotter; lower it and it boils cooler. The boiling temperature at a given pressure is the
. Water at that temperature is
; colder water is
; steam hotter than it is
So a drum is a pot of boiling water: its temperature is fixed by its pressure. That is why the HRSG course classifies a start by
: it tells you how hot the thick drum metal is.
Superheat = steam temperature − saturation temperature. HP main steam at 560.7 °C with a drum at 327 °C has about
of superheat. Superheated steam carries no water droplets, which would erode turbine blades or cause water hammer.
Turning water at its boiling point into steam takes a lot of heat without changing temperature: about
at atmospheric pressure,
at HP drum pressure. The reverse is
: steam touching colder metal gives all that heat back at once. That is why a drum's steam-filled top heats faster than its water-filled bottom during a start.
If the pressure on saturated water drops, the water is suddenly above its new boiling point and part of it boils at once. That is
. Flash tanks use it on purpose (blowdown water flashes to steam at lower pressure). In a drum it happens by accident whenever pressure dips.
Cold water weighs about
. Water at HP drum conditions weighs about
, and HP steam about
. A steam-water mixture is lighter than solid water.
From the drum, water falls down unheated pipes (
) into the heated

tubes. There part of it boils. The steam-water mixture is lighter than the water in the downcomers, so it rises back up to the drum. Nothing pumps it; density does the work. If the drum level falls too far, the downcomers stop being fed and the tubes can run dry and overheat.

ul: load rises → steam is drawn faster → drum pressure dips → water flashes → more bubbles in the tubes push water up into the drum → the level
, even though water is being used faster. Heating a cold drum at startup does the same as bubbles form.
load falls → pressure rises → bubbles collapse → the level
. Cold feedwater added fast also collapses bubbles.

p: Both are temporary, and both mislead an operator who reacts only to the level. That is why feed is controlled on steam flow as well as level (three-element control, Module 7).

case: Morning start: the HP drum local gauge reads 0.38 MPa. Is this a cold, warm or hot start for the HP drum?
steps: From the curve or table, water at 0.48 MPa boils at about 150 °C.
The HRSG course: HP drum cold < 100 °C, warm 100–280 °C, hot > 280 °C. 150 °C is warm.
Why pressure tells you metal temperature
A drum holding pressure is full of saturated water and steam, so its temperature is fixed by its pressure, and the thick wall has settled to about that temperature.

q: Steam leaves the IP superheater at 321 °C. IP drum pressure 3.21 MPa absolute (saturation 238 °C). How much superheat?

why: Superheat is above saturation, not the absolute temperature.
That is HP and reheat steam temperature.

q: Load rises quickly. For about a minute the drum level goes UP. Why?

text: Pressure dips, water flashes, bubbles push the level up (swell).

why: Swell happens before any feed change.

q: What drives water through the evaporator tubes?

why: Feed pumps push water into the drum; they don't drive the evaporator loop.

text: The difference in density between downcomer water and the steam-water mixture in the heated tubes.

why: The turbine draws steam from the superheater outlet, not through the evaporator.

q: Why does the steam-filled top of a cold drum heat faster than the water-filled bottom during startup?

text: Steam condensing on the cold metal releases its latent heat.
why: Right. Condensation delivers large amounts of heat quickly.

text: Steam is hotter than the water.
why: In a drum both are at saturation temperature.

text: The top is closer to the gas.
why: Drums sit outside the gas path.

q: Hot water at 0.54 MPa and 155 °C is let into a tank at atmospheric pressure. What happens?

text: Part of it flashes to steam at once.
why: 155 °C is above 100 °C, the boiling point at atmospheric pressure.
The pressure drop makes it boil immediately.

title: Bridge to the HRSG course
intro: These come straight from the HRSG course and manual. If you can answer them, you are ready for the parts of that course that rely on this module.

q: HRSG course: at startup, fill the HP drum to about −250 mm, well below normal. Why?

text: Heating makes bubbles that swell the level, so it needs room to rise.
why: Right. Swell at first boiling would otherwise push the level towards the high trip.

text: Because the gauge reads high when cold.

q: HRSG course: "Full water: superheated steam temperature drops suddenly." Why would a high drum level cool the steam?

text: Water droplets carried over into the superheater absorb heat as they boil off.

why: Feedwater enters the drum, not the superheater.
The cause is water in the superheater.

title: Metal under heat
goals: Calculate thermal expansion and explain why pipes and drums need room to move.
Explain thermal stress in thick walls, fatigue and creep.
Explain brittle behaviour when cold and thermal shock.

q: Guess: why does the HP drum (125 mm wall) have a slower heating limit than the superheater header?

text: A thicker wall develops a bigger inside-to-outside temperature difference, and so more stress, at the same heating rate.
The drum holds water, which heats slowly.
why: The limit is set by the metal, not the water.

p: Steel expands by about
). The HP drum is 15.1 m long. Heated from 20 °C to 327 °C it grows about:
Superheater tubes at 560 °C grow even more. If anything stops that growth, it bends pipes, cracks welds or tears supports. So pipes hang on
and
that let them slide, and drums and headers carry
: pointers that show how far they have moved. At startup you record them cold, then check the movement is what it should be.

image.alt: Metal bellows expansion joint in a pipeline
caption: A bellows compensator: it lets the pipe grow without pushing on the equipment.

p: Heat enters a drum from the inside. The inner surface heats first and tries to grow; the cooler outer part holds it back. That restraint is
. It grows with the temperature difference across the wall, and a thick wall has a bigger difference for the same heating rate. The HP drum wall is
: that is why it gets the slowest rate (under 5 °C/min).

The same happens top to bottom. If the top of a drum is much hotter than the bottom, the top grows more and the drum bends slightly like a banana. The stress concentrates at nozzles and welds. That is the reason for the
top-bottom limit.
One start does no visible damage. But each start-stop cycle stresses the same spots, and after enough cycles a crack starts. This is
. Rate limits don't prevent it; they slow it down so the drum lasts its design life.
At high temperature under stress, steel slowly stretches over years. This is

. It matters most for the hottest parts: superheater and reheater tubes at about 560 °C. Running just a little too hot for long periods eats creep life fast, which is why steam temperature has a high alarm (567.5 °C) close to normal (560.7 °C). That is also why the hottest sections use alloy steels such as P91/T91 and P22/T22, while cooler sections use carbon steel (SA-106C pipe, SA-210C tube).

ul: Carbon steel becomes less tough when cold. Under high pressure, cold steel can crack suddenly instead of stretching. That is why hydraulic test water must be at least

cold water hitting very hot metal cools the surface in seconds while the inside stays hot. The surface is pulled in tension and can crack. That is why you never refill an HRSG after a serious water shortage until the tubes have cooled.

case: An HP superheater header 8 m long runs at 560 °C. How much does it grow from 20 °C, and why does the manual want you to check hangers during startup?
steps: 8 m × 12×10⁻⁶ × 540 ≈ 0.052 m ≈ 52 mm. (Alloy steels expand a little differently; this is an estimate.)
The header and its pipes must slide about 5 cm. A seized hanger or a pipe resting on a steel beam blocks it.

The HRSG course asks you to check expansion of pipes, supports and hangers at 0.2–0.4 MPa and compare indicators with the cold record. A reading that stays at zero while others move means something is stuck.

q: Why do drums carry expansion indicators?

text: To show how far the drum has moved as it heats, so blocked expansion is spotted.

q: A superheater runs 10 °C above design for months. What damage mechanism does this speed up?

why: Creep life at high temperature drops quickly with small temperature increases.

q: Why is hydraulic test water required to be at least 20 °C?

text: Cold carbon steel is less tough and can crack suddenly under test pressure.
Cold water is too dense for the pumps.

q: Each startup and shutdown slightly damages the drum even when all limits are respected. What is this damage called?

why: Low-cycle fatigue from repeated thermal stress cycles.
Creep is slow stretching at steady high temperature.
Erosion is wear by flowing water or particles.

title: Bridge to the HRSG course

Water hammer is a steam-line problem.

p: Condenser → condensate pump → condensate heater → LP drum (deaerated) → HP or IP feed pump → economizer → drum → downcomer → evaporator → drum (steam separates) → superheater → main steam valve → turbine.

case: Trace a kilogram of water from the condenser until it reaches the IP turbine as reheated steam.
steps: Condenser → condensate pump → condensate heater (coldest end of the HRSG) → LP drum, where it is deaerated.

Down the downcomers, up through the HP evaporator, back into the drum as steam.
Steam leaves the drum through three HP superheater stages (spray between stages 2 and 3) to about 560 °C.
HP turbine → back to the HRSG as cold reheat → reheater to about 560 °C → IP turbine.

p: An impeller spins the water fast; the casing turns that speed into pressure. Key ideas:

ul: at the impeller eye pressure is lowest. If it falls below the water's saturation pressure, bubbles form and then collapse violently further in, eating the metal and shaking the pump. Hot water is close to boiling, so it cavitates easily.

(net positive suction head): how much margin above boiling the water has at the pump inlet. The pump needs a minimum (NPSHr); the system must supply more (NPSHa). elevation, far above the feed pumps.
a pump running with almost no flow heats the trapped water until it flashes. A minimum-flow (recirculation) valve always lets some flow back to the suction.

case: Why is the HP feed pump so sensitive to a low LP drum level, when the LP drum still holds plenty of water?
steps: Water from the LP drum at its boiling point (about 163 °C at its 0.67 MPa working pressure).
Water already at its boiling point has no margin from temperature. The only margin is the height of water above the pump (static head).
A lower level means less head, so less NPSH available. The pump approaches cavitation.
That is why the HRSG course checks LP drum level before starting feed pumps, and why the LP drum trip is set where it is.

q: Which valve type should not be used half-open to throttle flow?

why: Gate valves are for isolation only.
Control valves are made to sit partly open.

q: What is a minimum-flow valve for?

text: Keeping enough water flowing through the pump to carry away heat when forward flow is low.

q: What does moving the scoop tube of a hydraulic coupling do?

text: Changes the oil level in the coupling and so the pump speed.

why: The motor runs at constant speed.

q: A motor insulation reading is low after rain got into its terminal box. Likely cause?

why: Moisture is the most common cause of low insulation resistance.

q: Noise like gravel inside a pump, with vibration and falling discharge pressure. Most likely?

why: Collapsing vapour bubbles sound like gravel.
That would stop flow, but the gravel sound points to cavitation.

case: At 20% load the feedwater flow reading jumps around by ±15 t/h, while at 90% load it is steady. Is the flowmeter broken?
steps: An orifice plate: DP rises with the square of flow.

This is why level control uses single-element at low load and three-element at higher load, and why the HRSG course lets you drop from three-impulse to single when it becomes unstable.

q: Guess: why does salt build up in a drum even if feedwater is almost pure?

text: Only pure steam leaves, so everything dissolved stays and concentrates.
why: Right. Blowdown removes the concentrated water.
Corrosion releases iron, not the salts meant here.

p: When water boils in a drum, only pure steam leaves. Everything dissolved stays behind and concentrates. Even small amounts of salt in feedwater build up to scale on tubes (which then overheat), corrosion, and foaming. So the plant uses
water, with almost all dissolved salts removed, and bleeds concentrated drum water out as

What it is
Why operators care

rising conductivity = contamination or poor blowdown

p: Dirty drum water (high dissolved or suspended solids, oil) foams. Foam and high level let water droplets leave with the steam:
. The steam temperature drops as droplets boil off in the superheater, and salts go to the turbine. Signs: rising sodium or conductivity in steam, falling steam temperature, a swinging level.
Samples are taken continuously from feed, drum water and steam through
(which need cooling water) into analysers. Sampling lines are flushed at startup because stagnant lines give false readings.

h: Why chemistry can stop a startup

p: If steam fails specification, sending it to the turbine deposits silica and salts on the blades. So the HRSG course says: until chemistry passes, no steam to the turbine; blow down and dose instead.

A shut-down HRSG corrodes wherever oxygen and water meet bare steel. Every preservation method removes one of them: dry it, fill it with alkaline (ammonia) water, blanket it with nitrogen, or put desiccant inside.

steps: Sodium doesn't evaporate. Its presence in steam means drum water droplets are getting into the steam.
High level and a small temperature drop fit carry-over.
Carry-over from high level (or foaming if water quality is also poor).
Bring the level back to normal, tell chemistry, check drum water conductivity, increase continuous blowdown if they ask. This is the HRSG course's full-water and foaming territory.

why: Sodium in steam is a warning.

head: Module
Assumed knowledge taught there
rows: GT, HRSG, steam turbine, condenser and how they connect; "no supplementary firing"; 2×1 / 3×1; combining steam; turbine HP/IP/LP bypass; three-way damper and bypass stack; cold and hot reheat; condenser vacuum; sliding pressure; GT load as the HRSG's heat source
MPa.a vs MPa(g) vs plain MPa; bar and kPa; mmH₂O; t/h vs kg/s; Nm³/min; drum level in mm from a datum and NWL±; °C/min and MPa/min; ppm, ppb, µS/cm, pH, MΩ, mm²/s, dB(A); vibration in mm

saturation temperature and its link to pressure; start types by drum saturation temperature; superheat; latent heat; condensation heating; flashing; densities; natural circulation; swell and shrink; carry-over; why steam must be dry for the turbine

thermal expansion and expansion indicators; hangers and supports; thermal stress in thick walls; drum top-bottom ΔT and bowing; fatigue; creep; alloy vs carbon steels (P91, T22, SA-106C); brittle behaviour when cold; thermal shock

economizer, evaporator, superheater stages, reheater, condensate heater, fin tubes; drum and internals; downcomers, risers, headers; deaerator; continuous vs periodic blowdown; flash tanks; EDV; vents, drains, air valves; desuperheaters; casing, insulation, guard sheath; manholes; stack

gate, globe, check, butterfly, control, motor-operated, safety and relief valves; bypass valves; primary and secondary valves; packing and glands; gags; centrifugal pumps; cavitation and NPSH; minimum flow and recirculation; venting pumps; hydraulic coupling and scoop tube; sliding vs rolling bearings; oil cups; mechanical seals; vibration; listening rod; megger; rotation check; standby auto-start

4–20 mA; transmitters; orifice flow and its low-flow weakness; DP level with balance vessel and density correction; bi-colour, electric-contact, magnetic flap gauges; DCS, EWS, forcing and simulation; local/remote; auto/manual; feedback; PID; single- vs three-element ("impulse") control; alarm vs interlock vs trip vs permissive

demineralised water; concentration in drums; blowdown; pH, conductivity, oxygen, silica, sodium, iron, copper, hardness; hydrazine, phosphate, ammonia dosing; foaming and carry-over; sample coolers and analysers; why chemistry stops a startup; lay-up principles

work permits and their closure; isolation and test position; steam, hot water, stored pressure, gauge glass, confined space, noise and chemical hazards; shift leader, main operator, vice operator, walk inspector; repeat-back and report-back; logbook; handover during faults

P&ID symbols and instrument letters; general arrangement drawings; KKS codes; the manual's translated terms: door/gate, air door, furnace, pot, vaporizer, MP/medium-voltage, impulse, fixed value, rolling, combining steam, attemperating water, thimble/card, listening stick, sundries, walk inspector, starter, latch off, coasting, reignite, chromatic cycle

p: Thermodynamic cycle calculations, detailed turbine and generator theory, electrical protection, and gas turbine operation. The HRSG course doesn't need them. They belong in the prerequisites for a gas turbine or steam turbine course, which could reuse Modules 1–4 and 6–10 of this one unchanged.
